name: Docker, Inc. (formerly dotCloud)
origin_detail: Started in 2008 as dotCloud, a platform-as-a-service founded by Solomon Hykes and colleagues in Paris that later went through Y Combinator and moved to San Francisco. It open-sourced its internal container tool as Docker in March 2013 and renamed itself Docker, Inc. that year.
openness_notes: Docker Engine was Apache-2.0 and became the Moby project (2017); runc went to the Open Container Initiative and containerd to CNCF, so the runtime core is foundation-governed. Docker Desktop is proprietary and since August 2021 requires a paid subscription for larger companies; Docker Hub is a SaaS. Level 2.

license_history.license: Docker Desktop: paid subscription required for larger companies

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Pushed some users to alternatives such as Podman Desktop and Rancher Desktop (unverified)

exit_events.note: Mirantis bought the Docker Enterprise business in November 2019; Docker, Inc. restructured around developer tools (unverified; value deliberately null)

risk_events: 2019: Enterprise unit sold to Mirantis and company restructured after failing to monetize containers at scale (unverified)
2021: Desktop licence change for larger companies (unverified)
robustness: The container runtime and image formats are governed by OCI and CNCF, so the technology does not depend on Docker, Inc.; the company's paid products (Desktop, Hub) are proprietary.
openness_effect_assessment: Not assessed: no sourced research was possible in this session.
key_takeaway: Draft only. Docker's open-source project won its market so completely, and gave key pieces to foundations (OCI, CNCF), that the company struggled to capture the value: Kubernetes and the clouds monetized containers, Docker sold its enterprise unit in 2019 and rebuilt around paid developer subscriptions. Valuation and revenue need sourcing.
